newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Base metals rollercoaster as coffee slips.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Base metals rollercoaster as coffee slips.

text.p: A mixed day across commodities markets on Thursday saw coffee retrace from Wednesday's rally and base metals end higher after drifting lower early on.
Coffee futures in London were down from Wednesday's nine-month high, but traders said the outlook remained uncertain and sharp swings in New York could continue to dictate London prices.
Benchmark May robusta futures closed at $1,735 per tonne, after at one point touching $1,820 on Wednesday, sparking some European roasters to increase retail prices.
In New York, arabica coffee futures fell to a low of $1.98 per pound, down from Wednesday's much-eyed 27-month high of $2.00 per pound.
Recent strength in coffee, which has risen by 50 percent in London since the start of the year, has mostly been fuelled by supply worries.
Analysts said coffee prices could be overdue for a pause, but with the bullish trend continuing, it was hard to pinpoint any firm direction.
And while the fundamental supply picture for robustas looked less bright, dealers said they could benefit from a surge in demand as roasters switch from arabicas where low harvests are forecast.
Robustas could, however, come under pressure from fresh harvest from Indonesia, traders said.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME), a lack of market-moving news left base metal prices swinging around in choppy trading, with late surges in copper and aluminium reversing earlier weakness.
Dealers said after an undecided market all day, when buying finally came in, everybody rushed in.
Three-months copper rose above $2,400 per tonne in late trading, settling at $2,403 per tonne, up $28 on the day, after fund-buying into midday dips spurred the price up.
Aluminium also picked up late in the day to close at $1,689 after an earlier low of $1,655.
"Copper and aluminium have been well supported by the trade and specs today," said analyst Robin Bhar of Brandeis. "These metals don't seem to want to go lower."
Strong U.S. factory and durable goods orders may have encouraged funds to buy metals.
But early trade was so light that one dealer said: "It's so slow it feels like August."
A spate of profit-taking had taken prices lower on Wednesday, and traders and some analysts said a downside correction in copper and aluminium was overdue after recent gains.
Zinc and nickel also showed last-minute gains.

Nickel dealers awaited news on a labour dispute at Russia's Arctic Norilsk nickel complex. Earlier, a Norilsk spokesman said they hoped to reach an agreement with trade unions after workers planned strikes on March 27 and April 2.

Market concern early this week over possible disruption to supplies from Russia were allayed by news that Trans-World Group, a major foreign investor in Russian metal, planned to invest $500 million in Russian aluminium smelters.
Palladium was the only precious metals to end the day up, with gold finishing unchanged from Wednesday despite a brief intraday high.
The gold market remained depressed following Wednesday's tumble, on news that Switzerland proposed to sell around 40 tonnes of gold bullion reserves to set up a fund for Holocaust victims.
Dealers said while the move by Switzerland did not cause them much concern, they were worried other central banks could follow suit.
"The Swiss move may give impetus to use gold to finance other good causes," said analyst Andy Smith of Union Bank of Switzerland. "Who's next? What cause is next?" he asked.
Crude oil finished the day down, failing to hold on to a burst of strength fuelled by a bounce in New York. Benchmark Brent April futures were at $19.50 a barrel, down slightly from Wednesday.
Dealers cited poor physical demand, and news of increased production for the bearish tone.

In the grain market, prices lacked movement as fears that supply could be hit by Brazilian dockworkers striking in the key grain port of Paranagua were allayed when a union director said the action would not spread to other ports.
